https://www.internazionale.it/ultime-not.body:
PARIS, Oct 23 (Reuters) - A gunman who officials suspect may have been motivated by Islamophobic hatred opened fire from a car west of Paris on Friday, killing one person and wounding four others, including a 12-year-old girl.

“The investigations are ongoing, but it is clearly a terrorist crime. It is an extremely serious act,” Interior Minister Laurent Nunez told reporters from the Yvelines district west of Paris where the attack took place.

Officials said the 39-year-old suspect, who has not been named, drove through the town of Trappes, where he fired an automatic weapon at a petrol station, a medical centre and a children’s playground.

Broadcaster BFM said the wounded girl had been hit eight times and was in a serious condition.

“(It was) objectively a racist attack, probably Islamophobic,” said Ali Rabeh, the mayor of Trappes, whose parents came from Morocco. “The people targeted today could just as easily have been my mother, my brothers or my sisters-in-law.”

Police managed to arrest the man before he could injure anyone else. Video images showed his car riddled with bullets.

The shooting comes at a moment of particular tension in France, after nationwide protests turned violent last Saturday and before further demonstrations this coming weekend.

Some far-right politicians have blamed immigration for the wave of looting and vandalism that battered a number of French cities on October 17.

Rabeh, who is a left-wing politician, called for a collective condemnation of rhetoric that “ideologically arms those capable of carrying out such acts”.

The anti-terrorism prosecutor’s office, known as PNAT, said its investigation included looking at whether the shooting was racially or religiously motivated.

PNAT can take over any criminal investigation it believes meets the criteria for terrorism, including violence inspired by far-right ideas. Terrorism sentences are tougher, and counter-terrorism forces have greater investigative powers.

Nicolas Dainville, the mayor of nearby La Verriere, said the suspect lived in the town of Plaisir, which is also in Yvelines, and was “of a European type”. Rabeh said two of the victims were of African and North African origin, respectively, and did not provide details about the backgrounds of the other victims.

(Reporting by Juliette Jabkhiro, Dominique Vidalon, Zhifan Liu and Sudip Kar-Gupta; Writing by Crispian Balmer, Editing by Makini Brice and Peter Graff)

https://hromadske.ua/en/world/273049-ger.body:
Disruptions to shipping routes in the Middle East and the Black Sea could lead to famine in poorer countries if essential supplies of food and fertilizer fail to arrive, German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul warned on October 23.

Speaking ahead of talks with fellow foreign ministers in Istanbul, Wadephul said attacks on maritime trade were already affecting consumers worldwide through higher fuel and food costs, Deutsche Welle reported.

"We're all feeling the effects of the attacks on shipping lanes, whether at the gas station or in the supermarket," he said. "But elsewhere, there is a threat of famine when fertilizers don't arrive in the places where they are essential for basic production."

Wadephul pointed to three areas of concern: Iran's closure of the Strait of Hormuz, threats from Yemen's Houthi movement near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, and Russian attacks on shipping in the Black Sea.

The disruptions threaten countries that rely heavily on imported wheat and fertilizers, he said, singling out Turkey as a major wheat-processing country.

"We will not accept Iran and the Houthi militias holding global trade hostage," Wadephul said, calling for attacks on commercial shipping to stop.

Russia's attacks on Ukrainian ports and civilian vessels have also disrupted grain exports in recent months.

In July, Ukrainian agricultural company Kernel suspended operations at terminals in the port of Chornomorsk following Russian strikes. In August, a Russian attack on a cargo ship carrying Ukrainian wheat killed a Ukrainian sailor.

Further attacks in October struck vessels transporting corn and rapeseed oil, adding to concerns about the safety of commercial shipping in the Black Sea.

Wadephul was traveling to Istanbul for discussions with foreign ministers from Turkey, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, Egypt, France and the United Kingdom.

https://www.tovima.com/politics/kikilias.heading: Kikilias Says Greece Will Not Yield on Sovereign Rights - tovima.com

Athens is seeking to counter opposition claims of a “national defeat” over the Turkey-Libya agreement by emphasizing international law and accelerating talks with Egypt on expanding their maritime boundaries

Minister of Maritime Affairs and Insular Policy Vassilis Kikilias has said Greece will not compromise on its sovereign rights amid renewed tensions over the 2019 maritime agreement between Turkey and Libya, describing foreign policy as an ongoing struggle that cannot be won or lost in a single day.

Speaking to Greek broadcaster SKAI, Kikilias also discussed government plans to support ferry services as fuel costs rise, ways to increase the economic benefits of Greece’s shipping industry and recent allegations of misconduct in Greek basketball.

Kikilias said he had submitted a proposal to the prime minister’s office and the Finance Ministry to help the ferry industry manage rising fuel costs and keep ticket prices stable.

He emphasized the importance of maintaining connections between Greece’s islands, particularly during the winter, when ferries carry fewer passengers but remain essential for residents and the transportation of goods.

“I am glad that, based on my proposal, you have heard the prime minister’s statements,” Kikilias said, adding that institutional meetings with representatives of the industry were expected in the coming period to determine how support would be provided.

He said several policy tools were available despite the country’s difficult fiscal circumstances and urged European institutions to give member states room to help their citizens.

“We will not depart from our fiscal commitments to Europe and those who make the decisions, I agree. But there must also be an understanding of the crisis we are facing,” he said.

Kikilias noted that ferry ticket prices did not rise in 2025, despite the industry announcing planned increases of around 15%. Prices also remained stable in 2026 amid the war in the Middle East, following €60 million in support approved by the government’s economic team and the prime minister after his proposal.

He said the government would do everything possible to support ferry services serving smaller islands and routes that are not commercially viable without public assistance.

Kikilias also highlighted opportunities to translate Greece’s strength in global shipping into broader economic benefits for domestic businesses.

Referring to his recent trip to Japan and China, where he met government officials and shipping industry representatives, he said Greece’s position as the world’s largest shipping power gave it significant weight in Asian markets.

He noted that Greek-owned vessels account for 68% of shipbuilding activity in China, citing the figure as an example of the sector’s scale.

During his meetings, Kikilias said he asked for Greek marine equipment manufacturers to receive preference when equipment is purchased for ships being built in those countries. He also called for closer ties that would allow Greece’s shipping strength to generate greater returns across the domestic economy.

He described the Shipping and Island Policy Ministry as an economic development ministry, with responsibilities extending beyond ferry connections, migration and maritime border enforcement.

He also pointed to port infrastructure and the development of Greek ports as opportunities to strengthen tourism, yachting and the cruise industry, bringing benefits to local communities.

Turning to the Turkey-Libya maritime memorandum, Kikilias said the agreement was not a new development, noting that it was signed in November 2019 by the government in western Libya.

He described the agreement as unlawful and said its recent ratification by Libya’s House of Representatives reflected the influence Turkey had built in the country. He also referred to the removal of the parliament’s speaker.

Kikilias said the latest development was unwelcome but should not be treated as decisive for Greece’s foreign policy.

“I do not believe that anyone loses in foreign policy in a single day or wins in a single day. It is a constant struggle and a major effort,” he said.

He called for serious policymaking, a clear and professional approach, and for those with the necessary expertise to lead discussions. He added that people who are not involved in negotiations do not have the full picture.

“As a member of this government, I have said many times, regarding Turkey, that when it comes to our sovereign rights, we will not take even one step back,” he said.

Kikilias, a former international basketball player, also described recent revelations about Greek basketball as “a disgrace” and called for the investigation to proceed without prejudging anyone’s guilt.

He said the authorities should establish the facts methodically and determine who, if anyone, was involved, stressing the importance of the presumption of innocence.

Kikilias said allegations of misconduct risk undermining children’s confidence in sports and the fairness of competition. Children should be able to win or lose a game and leave with their heads held high, he said, trusting that the rules are applied fairly.

He described the issue as a serious structural problem in a field that should promote healthy values. He praised the sports judge and those who conducted the investigation, calling for it to continue to its conclusion.

Kikilias also warned against a growing perception that everyone in public life or institutions is equally implicated in wrongdoing.

“I do not agree with that, and I do not accept it. I want to say that everyone is equal, yes, but not everyone is the same,” he said.

He called for allegations involving organizations, political parties or public bodies to be investigated by the judiciary, rather than through public condemnation.

“Not public uproar and people’s courts. Justice,” he said.

https://www.euronews.com/2026/10/23/ital.body:
Nationwide protests against the rising cost of living are expected in Italy and France on Saturday 24 October. Authorities and business owners fear a repeat of what happened on 17 and 18 October, when hundreds of people were involved in violent incidents targeting shops and law enforcement.

Protests are planned in several Italian cities, including Milan, Bologna, Genoa, Turin, Rome and Florence. According to "Mappa della rivolta", a website that collates protest initiatives, more than 30 mobilisations are scheduled, ranging from marches and sit-ins to assemblies and strikes.

The capital will be under tight security for the occasion. Rome's police headquarters has drawn up a security plan to manage both notified demonstrations and spontaneous rallies announced online. In addition to the usual units deployed to handle protests, drones from the State Police's 1st Flight Department and aircraft from the Carabinieri will also be used. In all, around 1,500 officers will be deployed, with checks stretching from city squares to railway stations.

Rome's Cybersecurity Centre is also operational, monitoring posts and activities on social media in coordination with Digos, the specialized operational division of the Italian State Police.

The digital dimension is making it harder to manage the protests. On Telegram, TikTok and Instagram, guides on how to prepare for clashes are circulating. Advice ranges from bringing water, painkillers and vinegar to lessen the effects of tear gas, to guidance on what to wear and how to behave if disorder breaks out.

In Milan, there will be around one thousand police officers and Carabinieri, 300 municipal officers and 500 soldiers deployed following the latest government security decree. Here too, drones will be used to monitor the marches. Authorised demonstrations will take place away from the Duomo, while protests are banned in the Garibaldi and Porta Venezia districts.

In Turin, a demonstration is expected that has been organised by activists from the antagonista scene linked to the former Askatasuna social centre, together with members of the 17 October Movement and students. Marches are due to start at 2 p.m. in Piazza Arbarello.

Following the unrest on 17 October, on Friday Digos carried out searches targeting around 100 people, 51 of whom were minors. Operations took place in several cities, including Bari, Bergamo, Florence, Genoa and Verona.

“There were many temptations, including from some coalition partners, to make drastic cuts. Or to resort to certain tricks that might have been ill-considered and not coordinated with our defence partners,” Valys told LRT.lt in an interview.

Lithuania has committed to maintaining defence spending at a level in excess of 5% of GDP.

https://www.dutchnews.nl/2026/10/cyber-s.body:
The Netherlands’ National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) is investigating the first signs of successful hacks on websites following the exposure of critical vulnerabilities on the web, and says the situation could “rapidly worsen”.

A spokesperson told the Volkskrant on Thursday that the signals came from the NCSC’s international network, and that there was no sign yet of abuse involving Dutch websites. The centre is still checking whether the reports are accurate.

Cybersecurity researchers, working with the help of AI, found that PHP, the programming language on which a majority of the web is built, had at least two serious vulnerabilities in its code.

Details of the weaknesses were leaked online on Monday, and the PHP developers announced they would issue an upgrade by Wednesday afternoon.

Hacking attempts began even before the leak, with Amazon reporting an attack attempt on October 17. US internet security firm Cloudflare said it saw hacking attempts run from thousands before the upgrade to millions afterwards.

Initially, the NCSC said that there were no signs of active hacks and the PHP developers said there were no indications of breaches.

Large amounts of government, healthcare and news sites were forced to go dark temporarily while awaiting the upgrade, including Dutch News.

The Netherlands was fast to act, closing a large amount of its sites and issuing warnings early on Wednesday, after which governments in Belgium, Germany, France and Finland did the same. The issue is now a global concern.

Dutch privacy watchdog AP said on Thursday it had not yet received any reports of data breaches linked to the vulnerabilities.

https://nltimes.nl/2026/10/23/dutch-emba.body:
The Dutch embassy in the Egyptian capital of Cairo is closed to the public until further notice. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs made this decision following nine days of demonstrations against the Netherlands at the embassy, the embassy said on Facebook.

The protesters are demonstrating against the Dutch police arresting Ahmed Nasser, the deputy head of the Union of Egyptian Youth Abroad and a spokesperson for the government, NOS reports. He was arrested on October 10, reportedly for threatening an activist in the Netherlands, and his pre-trial detention has since been extended.

The Egyptian government typically does not tolerate protests, so the ones at the embassy are likely not spontaneous. According to NOS, protesters are dropped off daily by bus. At each protest, the embassy had to be evacuated for security reasons.

According to NOS, Nasser was arrested for threatening activist Anas Habib, who gained notoriety this summer when he used a padlock to lock the gate of the Egyptian embassy in The Hague. Habib filmed the act, saying it was a protest against Egypt keeping the Rafah border crossing with Gaza closed to Palestinians trying to flee Israeli attacks. His protest triggered a chain reaction, and activists locked the gates of Egyptian embassies in several other countries.

A short time later, a video leaked showing the Egyptian Minister of Foreign Affairs addressing the ambassador in the Netherlands. “I’ve said a hundred times, whoever touches the [embassies] should be held accountable,” the Minister says. He goes on to say that if anyone is caught touching the embassy’s fence, “drag him inside” and “give him hell.”

It is unclear when the Dutch embassy in Egypt will reopen. It remains accessible for consular assistance in case of emergencies.

Katarzyna Pełczyńska-Nałęcz, the leader of a junior party in Poland’s ruling coalition, has announced that her resignation from the government and the leadership of her party, the centrist Poland 2050 (Polska 2050), in protest over a parliamentary vote on Thursday.

Pełczyńska-Nałęcz, who serves as minister for funds and regional policy, made her decision in the wake of an unusual voting result in the Sejm, the more powerful lower house of parliament, on Thursday.

Another junior partner in the ruling coalition, the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL), had proposed a bill abolishing two-term limits for mayors. Those limits had been introduced in 2018 with the aim of reducing corruption and cronyism by preventing local officials from becoming entrenched in power.

However, PSL, which has a strong presence in local politics, argues that the limits prevent effective, popular mayors from being re-elected, thereby denying voters the right to decide who they want to represent them.

Although the government has a majority in the Sejm, the bill was narrowly defeated, with 213 votes in favour and 215 against, after 15 MPs from the ruling coalition joined with the right-wing opposition in voting against it.

How MPs from each parliamentary group voted on the bill ( za = for, przeciw = against, wstrzymało się = abstained, nie głosowało = did not vote)

Pełczyńska-Nałęcz herself is not a member of parliament, so did not vote. Her party was split, with six MPs voting for the bill, three against, three abstaining, and three not voting at all.

Aftewards, Pełczyńska-Nałęcz made clear that she opposed the bill and celebrated the fact that it was blocked. She also announced her resignation from the government and the leadership of her party.

“The coalition, unfortunately including a significant portion of MPs from Poland 2050, stood against the people and in favour of backroom political deals,” she wrote. “I am leaving Donald Tusk’s government because values are more important to me than positions.”

“I am leaving the party in the hands of its founder, who stepped away but then returned,” she added, referring to Poland 2050’s founder, Szymon Hołownia. “I hope that he remembers what values he came to power in the name of.”

Pełczyńska-Nałęcz’s decision follows a year of turmoil for Poland 2050. In September 2025, Hołownia, who had led the party since founding it in 2021, announced that he was stepping down.

However, a first attempt to choose a new leader was invalidated in January after technical problems with voting. Hołownia then hinted that he may reverse course and seek to continue leading the party, though in the end that did not happen.

In February, Pełczyńska-Nałęcz was chosen as the new leader. That prompted her rival candidate, Paulina Hennig-Kloska, to quit the party, taking half of its MPs with her. They formed a new group called Centrum (Centre).

Both Poland 2050 and Centrum remain in the ruling coalition. However, Pełczyńska-Nałęcz has had an uneasy relationship with Tusk.

On Friday, Tusk, who is on a state visit to India, sarcastically responded to Pełczyńska-Nałęcz’s resignation by saying, “I thought she’d at least call before she left”. He admitted that “cooperation \[with her\] has not been the easiest for a long time”.

The prime minister, however, added that he “does not think \[her resignation\] will have any impact on the future work of the coalition…My intuition tells me that this is her individual decision”.

Hołownia, who currently serves as head of Poland 2050’s parliamentary caucus, confirmed at a press conference on Friday alongside fellow MPs that the party intends to remain in Tusk’s coalition. But he also warned that, without Poland 2050, the government would not have a parliamentary majority.

The episode highlights the tensions within the ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right and contains parties that disagree on a number of issues.

It also points to the pressure smaller coalition partners are feeling ahead of next autumn’s parliamentary elections. Only parties that win at least 5% of the vote nationally can enter parliament. But Poland 2050 has been polling at around 1% and PSL is on 3%.

In the 2023 election, Poland 2050 and PSL in fact stood together as an alliance called the Third Way (Trzecia Droga), helping ensure that the two parties won enough votes to enter parliament. However, in 2025, they split from one another and confirmed that they would not stand together again.

In the wake of yesterday’s vote, PSL immediately announced that it would push for the introduction of two-term limits for members of parliament, arguing that the same rules should apply to national and local elected representatives.

The right-wing opposition has long hoped that it could tempt PSL, the most conservative element of Tusk’s coalition, to quit the government. A recent report even claimed that US President Donald Trump had, at the behest of Poland’s opposition, suggested to PSL’s leader that he leave Tusk.

The European Parliament and Romania’s Supreme Council for National Defense (CSAT) called for stronger measures to address escalating security threats in the Black Sea following attacks on civilian vessels and repeated airspace violations. Both mentioned the need for closer cooperation with NATO allies, improved drone detection, and faster implementation of the EU’s planned regional maritime security hub.

The European Parliament announced that it adopted its resolution on Thursday, October 22, with 432 votes in favor, 52 against, and 88 abstentions. MEPs condemned the latest deadly strikes off the Romanian and Bulgarian coasts and held Russia responsible for escalating its war against Ukraine into the western Black Sea.

The attacks were described as part of a “clear pattern of Russian escalation” involving the systematic targeting of civilian shipping.

Moreover, the MEPs called on the EU and its member states to consider deploying a naval operation in the Black Sea.

The resolution also urged NATO to consider a Black Sea initiative based on discussions about a possible “Black Sea Sentry” and called for closer cooperation among Romania, Bulgaria, and Türkiye.

EU countries, working with NATO, should provide further assistance to Romania and Bulgaria for the early detection and tracking of hostile drones, MEPs said. They also proposed using unspent funds from the SAFE defense instrument to help the two countries address regional threats.

Separately, Romania’s CSAT met at Cotroceni Palace under president Nicușor Dan on Thursday to assess the same escalation and the measures already taken. The council described recent attacks and airspace violations as “direct consequences of the Russian Federation’s aggression beyond Ukraine’s borders.”

CSAT said the situation posed immediate risks to human life, access to Romanian ports, and energy infrastructure in the country’s exclusive economic zone.

Thus, the Council decided that Romania’s priorities will include accelerating the development of maritime surveillance, mine countermeasure capabilities, and systems able to respond to drones entering national airspace or territorial waters. On Tuesday, Pakistan's military chief, Field Marshal Asim Munir, met Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf and security chief Mohsen Rezaei in Tehran.

Munir has also cultivated a close relationship with President Donald Trump, including meetings at the White House.

Pakistan has taken a direct military role in Saudi Arabia's defense.

Reuters reported in May that Islamabad had deployed approximately 8,000 troops, a squadron of fighter jets and air-defense systems to the kingdom under a bilateral agreement. Saudi Arabia financed the deployment, according to Pakistani officials cited by Reuters.

Pakistan’s commitment to Saudi security deepened in August when Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkey signed the Makkah Joint Defense Agreement, treating an attack against one member as an attack against all.

This week, Islamabad announced that Pakistan and Saudi Arabia had completed ratification, while Turkey's remained pending. The partners have also discussed further military mobilization following attacks by Iran-aligned Houthis on Saudi territory.

On Wednesday, Pakistan signed another defense agreement, this time with Turkey, Qatar and Indonesia. The Badr agreement, signed in Doha, offers opportunities for industrial cooperation and defense production.

Together with Makkah, the agreements deepen Pakistan's military, diplomatic and economic ties across countries pursuing different regional agendas.

That tension was evident during Munir's Tehran visit. Pakistani government sources told Turkey's state-run Anadolu news agency that the talks focused more on stopping Houthi attacks against Saudi Arabia than on reviving US-Iran negotiations.

Munir pressed Iranian leaders to use their influence over the Houthis, citing Pakistan's commitment to defend the kingdom.

Saudi Arabia and other Persian Gulf states supply much of Pakistan’s energy, while millions of Pakistani workers live in the region. Defense cooperation brings financial support and industrial opportunities, while diplomacy helps protect relations with competing partners.

Pakistan appears to be carving out an unusual role: mediating between Iran and the United States, helping defend Saudi Arabia against the Houthis, and joining new regional defense ventures while retaining direct access to Iranian leaders.

But the same network could become harder to manage if regional tensions escalate. The more security commitments Pakistan assumes, the greater the chance that relationships which currently give Islamabad leverage could eventually force it to choose between them.

https://www.defensenews.com/global/midea.body:
Saudi Arabia appears to be expanding its ballistic missile factory to build larger solid-fuel missiles that could fly farther or carry heavier payloads, according to two U.S. researchers who analyzed more than a year of commercial satellite images.

More capable missiles could help Saudi Arabia to deter attacks by Iran and make its military more self-reliant, while possibly strengthening its position in a deadly conflict with Yemen’s Tehran-backed Houthi fighters.

But they risk fueling a regional missile race and could deepen opposition in the U.S. Congress to a U.S.-Saudi civilian nuclear agreement that has already raised concerns about proliferation.

Satellite company Planet Labs, based in the U.S., took images of the al-Duwadimi complex about 125 miles west of Riyadh between April 2025 and September 2026.

The two researchers, Sam Lair and Michael Duitsman of the Foreign Policy Research Institute, assessed that those images show a new building that houses casting pits — wells in which a mixture of fuel ingredients is poured into missile motor casings and allowed to harden.

The Saudi embassy and Information Ministry did not respond to requests for comment.

The building, flanked by what appear to be walls to protect nearby structures from accidental explosions, is at least twice as large as the one believed to house the plant’s existing casting pits, Lair and Duitsman said in their assessment. The Foreign Policy Research Institute (FPRI) is a non-partisan research organization in Philadelphia.

A second new building could be used to store fuel ingredients or finished missile components, they said.

The imagery “suggests that Saudi Arabia is expanding the infrastructure at the missile production complex, likely to produce larger missiles which could deliver larger payloads or reach longer ranges,” they wrote.

Militaries favor solid-fuel missiles because they can be stored for long periods and launched more quickly than liquid-fuel systems.

Lair and Duitsman and experts from the London-based International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS) and the CNA research and analysis organization told Reuters that the makeup of Saudi Arabia’s missile force suggests that the al-Duwadimi complex relies on Chinese technology. Lair and Duitsman said that its characteristics are also similar to Chinese missile plants.

Saudi Arabia secretly acquired about 40 liquid-fuel DF-3 ballistic missiles from China in 1987, according to a 1991 declassified CIA estimate. It displayed two of them for the first time in an April 2014 military parade, according to a YouTube video and photographs of the event.

The FPRI team also recently identified from social media videos and photos what they assessed was the wreckage in Yemen of a Saudi-fired Chinese-designed DF-15 missile.

Lair said the kingdom may now be producing the solid-fuel DF-15, and that the expansion of a1-Dumadimi is likely for the production of the longer-range DF-21 or a similar missile.

Riyadh is believed to have turned to Beijing because Washington has long restricted exports of longer-range missile systems.

The Chinese embassy and defense ministry did not respond to requests for comment. The CIA declined to comment. The White House did not respond to a request for comment.

Sascha Bruchmann, a research fellow at IISS, said longer-range missiles would allow Saudi Arabia to strike Iran without risking its U.S.-supplied F-15 jet fighters against Iranian air defenses.

“You’d want a system to threaten whatever is holy to Tehran … if you don’t have the political will to send an F-15 with JDAMs over Tehran,” said Bruchmann, referring to U.S.-made satellite-guided bombs. “Iran has a lead because its missiles and drones can strike Saudi wherever it wants. The Saudis could close that capability gap a bit.”

Bruchmann, who reviewed the FPRI analysis at Reuters request, concurred that the expansion of al-Duwadimi could be for producing more powerful solid-fuel missiles.

Janes, the defense intelligence company, also reviewed it and said the buildings “may suggest an effort to expand production capability or support the development of longer-range missiles.”

Saudi Arabia’s apparent pursuit of more powerful missiles comes as other Gulf powers are also seeking to expand their offensive and defensive arsenals, said Decker Eveleth, a CNA analyst who has been tracking the al-Duwadimi construction with commercial satellite imagery and concurred with the FPRI assessment.

“This is being replicated across the Middle East,” he said. “You see exactly the same thing happening in the UAE. You see the exact same thing happening in Turkey. Everybody is doing this now.”

The expansion of al-Duwadimi could have political consequences in the US by stiffening bipartisan congressional opposition to a US-Saudi agreement under which the US would help Riyadh establish uranium enrichment for power generation.

Opponents say that the deal lacks sufficient safeguards to prevent Riyadh from secretly building a nuclear weapon. The kingdom has denied any such plan.

The FPRI assessment said the Planet Labs imagery showed that the expansion at al-Duwadimi began in April 2025 with ground-clearing and digging for the suspected storage building. Work on the suspected casting-pit building began later that month or in early May, it said.

A December 12, 2025, photo showed what researchers assessed were two deep pits inside the building that had no roof yet.

A Sept. 18, 2026, photo shows the roof still partly missing and “heavy duty blast diverting walls” on either side to prevent accidental explosions from damaging adjacent structures.

The walls, the researchers said, are somewhat similar to those depicted in imagery of US and Iranian missile plants and “further evidence the building is for casting solid propellant motors.”

Finishing the roofs would not take long, the FPRI said, but installing casting equipment may take several months. The facility could be ready to start producing missiles as early as the end of the year.

The memorandum was signed in November 2019 by Turkey and the then Tripoli-based Government of National Accord, led by Fayez al-Sarraj. It seeks to delimit maritime jurisdiction between Turkey and Libya in the Mediterranean and has been at the center of a long-running dispute over maritime boundaries and sovereign rights in the eastern Mediterranean.

According to Abdelatty’s account, Egypt reiterated its categorical rejection of the agreement’s ratification. Fidan, for his part, expressed understanding of the Egyptian side’s concerns and stressed the need for continued consultations to address them.

The meeting comes amid mounting regional opposition following the eastern Libyan parliament’s approval of the memorandum on Oct. 20, reversing its previous rejection of the agreements concluded with Ankara in 2019.

Cairo has argued that the memorandum violates international law, including the 1982 United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), and cannot have legal consequences for Egypt’s maritime rights. Egypt has also rejected any actions based on the agreement that conflict with its declared maritime boundaries.

Greece has likewise lambasted the memorandum, arguing that Turkey and Libya do not have opposite or adjacent coastlines that would provide a legal basis for the proposed delimitation and that the agreement flagrantly disregards the maritime entitlements of Greek islands, including Crete, the fifth-largest island in the Mediterranean. Athens has maintained that the Libyan parliament’s decision does not change the agreement’s legal status.

The dispute has also prompted Greece to raise the issue at the UN Security Council, while the European Union has reiterated that the memorandum infringes on the sovereign rights of third states, does not comply with the international law of the sea and is null and void.

Greece and Egypt signed an agreement partially delimiting their exclusive economic zones in August 2020. Both countries have stressed the importance of settling maritime-boundary disputes in accordance with international law and UNCLOS, while continuing diplomatic coordination over the implications of the Turkey-Libya memorandum.

Foreign ministers from eight countries met in İstanbul on Friday for their first talks in an expanded format on the Strait of Hormuz, conflicts across the Middle East and the Russia-Ukraine war.

Ministers from Britain, France and Germany — the so-called E3 — and Italy met their counterparts from the newly created R4 group of Turkey, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Egypt to discuss the Palestinians, developments in Yemen and Hormuz, and ways to end the Russia-Ukraine war, a Turkish foreign ministry source said.

The talks began at a hotel overlooking the Bosporus after separate meetings among the European ministers and their regional counterparts, the source added.

British Foreign Minister Ed Miliband’s office said the talks would focus on “the Strait of Hormuz and the situation in Saudi Arabia.”

Miliband “will advocate for a diplomatic solution to the [Hormuz] crisis that restores full navigational rights and freedoms,” his office said.

He will also stress “how Iranian tactics are being replicated across the region, with attacks on Saudi Arabia further destabilising the region and increasing pressure on vital waterways and global chokepoints, such as Bab El-Mandeb and the Suez Canal,” it added.

France confirmed the talks would address “the Iranian crisis in its various ramifications,” describing the meeting as a first “in this format … against a backdrop of extreme instability and uncertainty in the region.”

The aim is to “strengthen coordination between Europeans and Middle Eastern countries in the face of crises that we did not choose and that affect us all,” the French foreign ministry said.

Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan is hosting the meeting as Ankara seeks a stronger regional role, including through the Mecca Defence Alliance, a defense pact launched with Pakistan and Saudi Arabia in August.

Turkey says the pact is not directed against any specific country and remains open to other members, including Egypt.

Cairo has yet to decide whether to join. On Wednesday President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi said Egypt would “defend Saudi territory” and would not take part in any attack on Yemen.

Intensifying attacks by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis have forced Saudi Arabia to close its main airport and postpone a major investment conference. A maritime blockade has also threatened oil exports from the world’s largest crude exporter.

Riyadh has since secured support from its allies. During a surprise visit Wednesday, French President Emmanuel Macron said French forces would help protect the Red Sea oil terminal of Yanbu.

Britain announced a day earlier that it would deploy fighter jets to help defend Saudi Arabia against Houthi attacks.

Fidan praised regional cooperation Friday, saying, “Lasting solutions cannot be imposed from outside,” in an address to a mediation conference.

During the talks, he is expected to stress that countries in the region must “assume responsibility” for their security and that Turkey favors cooperation based on “regional ownership,” according to Turkish officials.

He is also expected to say that “existing disputes should not be allowed to feed one another, conflicts should not be allowed to spread to new areas, and regional tensions should not be allowed to turn into broader instability.”

On the Palestinians, Fidan is expected to call for increased international pressure on Israel over settlement expansion and what Ankara describes as “settler terrorism.”

He will also reiterate Turkey’s support for Saudi Arabia’s security against Houthi attacks and the need to safeguard freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab el-Mandeb.

The Black Sea is also on the agenda, with Fidan expected to highlight Turkey’s efforts to prevent the Russia-Ukraine war from spreading into the region.

https://www.internazionale.it/ultime-not.body:
Oct 23 (Reuters) - The first Russian diesel bound for the US following a surprise agreement reached between Moscow and US President Donald Trump is aboard a tanker heading for New York, ship-tracking data showed on Friday.

Trump announced the deal this month as part of his efforts to bring down soaring diesel prices ahead of November 3 US mid-term elections.

Trump also waived parts of a new US sanctions law against Russia and threatened Europe with a US diesel export ban unless countries released more from their emergency reserves to help ease prices.

The Malta-flagged medium-sized tanker Agioi Fanendes was loaded with 40,000 metric tons of ultra-low sulphur diesel in Russia’s Baltic port of Primorsk on October 22, according to LSEG shipping data. It is expected to arrive in the United States on November 7.

The identity of the buyer and seller were not immediately known. The cargo will be the first imported by the US since former President Joe Biden announced a ban on US imports of Russian oil and petroleum products in 2022.

Trump announced on October 9 that Russia would immediately export 300,000 metric tons, or 2.25 million barrels, to the US and global markets, followed by 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons “immediately thereafter”.

A Kremlin spokesperson on Friday confirmed a first ship under the deal had departed, but did not specify whether it was bound for the US market or elsewhere.

“As far as I’m aware, there have already been reports from the Ministry of Energy that the first tanker has, in fact, set sail for its recipients, its buyers. Further shipments will continue at a steady pace from here on,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on a daily conference call.

The deal with the US involved Russia lifting a self-imposed ban on diesel exports.

RUSSIA RESUMING GLOBAL EXPORTS Since the EU imposed a full embargo on imports of Russian oil products in February 2023 over the war in Ukraine, Russia has exported diesel mainly to Turkey and Brazil, as well as to African countries.

It also supplies Central Asia by rail.

Shipping data from LSEG and Kpler published this week showed Russian diesel cargoes resuming voyages to their traditional destinations after Moscow lifted its own ban, with at least two tankers signalling trips to Turkey and Brazil.

It was unclear where other tankers were destined for, with cargoes loaded in Primorsk signalling Gibraltar, the Atlantic Coast or Port-Said, LSEG data showed.

Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak has said additional US shipments would follow as companies from the two countries work out the necessary contracts.

Putin envoy Kirill Dmitriev, who also heads Russia’s sovereign wealth fund, said last week that the US Treasury had asked the fund to help sort out tricky payment issues relating to the agreement.

Novak has said that Russia would be able to increase its diesel exports to its usual levels of 3-3.5 million tons per month by year-end.

(Reporting by Reuters; editing by Philippa Fletcher and Jason Neely)

EU Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič said on Friday that the EU was walking a tightrope in negotiations with Beijing, weighing conventional trade measures against broader political considerations.

After several months of negotiations, Brussels and Beijing reached a deal on 9 October to curb imports of hybrid cars from China. However, the agreement is unlikely to significantly narrow the EU’s record trade deficit with China, which has reached €1 billion a day, a gap the European Commission is seeking to reduce.

“There are whole sectors under threat; each head of states and government is concerned that there might be potential heavy losses of the jobs,” Šefčovič said on Friday, after a meeting of the 27 trade ministers in Ireland.

He added: “We have to proceed not only with the traditional trade techniques, but also with a very political approach, how to balance the trade between between China and the European Union.”

A new round of discussions is taking place at a technical level with Beijing until the end of the year, with political negotiation scheduled for January and March 2027.

But given the urgency, EU leaders gave the European Commission a political mandate last week to work on a “kill switch” tool that would allow Europeans to cut off China's access to their market to counter economic distortions.

Under the October deal, the EU will introduce country-specific quotas allowing 350,000 Chinese hybrid cars onto the European market annually over four years, with a fixed annual adjustment rate of 6%.

The Commission aims to extend the agreement to other sectors, but EU officials warn that progress will also depend on Beijing’s response to the EU executive’s efforts to strengthen its trade defence tools.

The Commission is set to present a new instrument on 9 October aimed at encouraging EU companies to diversify their suppliers of strategic products to reduce their dependence on China.

It also hopes to present a proposal for the so-called “kill switch” that same week and ahead of the December summit of EU leaders. Pushed by France and Germany earlier this month, it would allow the Commission to adopt radical measures against Beijing in the event of economic pressure on the EU market.

Another unilateral EU trade defence measure targeting Chinese chemicals and industrial machinery could also come in December, with the risk of prompting Chinese countermeasures.

According to the latest Chinese customs data, China's exports to the EU have continued to surge, rising by 25% over the past year.

SEOUL — North Korean leader Kim Jong-un arrived in China on Saturday (Oct 24), visiting the neighbouring country via a newly opened bridge, a South Korean government official said.

Kim arrived in Dandong through the New Yalu River Bridge connecting North Korea and China, the official said on condition of anonymity as they are not authorised to speak publicly about the matter.

Chinese Premier Li Qiang met Kim in the border city, South Korea's Yonhap news agency said. Kim's visit comes a day before the anniversary of China joining the 1950-1953 Korean War.

China's foreign ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

China and North Korea opened the 3-km New Yalu River Bridge, their most significant land border crossing, this month after a long delay, aiming to rejuvenate trade and commerce after years of strained ties and ‌pandemic-related disruptions.

A visit by Kim now is consistent with the current phase of closer economic ties and more frequent high-level exchanges between China and North Korea, said Lu Chao, an expert in China-North Korea relations at the Liaoning Academy of Social Sciences, a Chinese government think-tank in Shenyang.

"The opening of the bridge has resolved a major bottleneck in China-North Korea trade logistics," Lu said. "With the logistics constraint eased, bilateral trade is likely to increase further."

The bridge is expected to help move heavy equipment, raw materials and energy products that North Korea needs for development. The opening is the latest sign of warming ties between Beijing and Pyongyang, after two summits between their leaders in the past 13 months.

Kim's last known visit to China was in September 2025, to attend the 80th Victory Day celebrations in Beijing, when he held a summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping. Xi made a state visit to North Korea in June.

"It is too early to divine Kim's intentions because he is only in Dandong," said Christopher Green, a Korea specialist at Leiden University in the Netherlands. "Will there be a Xi-Kim summit? Probably - it would be surprising if there were not. However, nothing is certain at this stage."

China, which fought alongside North Korea in the Korean War, is Pyongyang's main economic and diplomatic backer and accounts for most of its official trade. However, North Korea has drawn closer to Russia since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, which analysts say has reduced Pyongyang's reliance on Beijing.

US President Donald Trump has been eager to jump-start talks with North Korea, but US and South Korean officials see fading chances of him meeting Kim this year, Reuters reported on Friday.

China hosts a summit of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum next month in Shenzhen, which Trump is expected to attend.

South Korea renewed its offer Friday to hold military talks with North Korea to discuss their conflicting views on where the inter-Korean border sits, seeking to ease tensions sparked by last month's land mine blast inside the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ).

Seoul and Pyongyang have traded sharp rhetoric since South Korea blamed the North for the Sept. 21 mine blast inside the DMZ that injured three South Korean troops. Pyongyang has denied responsibility and vowed to take military actions along the border, if needed.

"Different perceptions remain over the Military Demarcation Line (MDL)," Deputy Defense Minister Kim Hong-cheol said in a press briefing, referring to the border separating the two Koreas.

"South Korea's Defense Ministry hereby officially proposes holding inter-Korean military talks with North Korean authorities to jointly verify the locations of the land-based MDL, restore military communication lines and discuss measures to prevent accidental clashes along the border," he said.

Kim said trilateral dialogue involving the U.N. Command (UNC), which administers and enforces the Armistice Agreement governing the border area, can also be considered.

This page has been blocked by an extension

"If necessary, a trilateral meeting including the UNC is also possible," he said. "We expect a positive response from the North's side."

The latest escalation of tensions comes amid Seoul's suspicions that North Korean forces have repeatedly crossed the MDL to carry out border fortification work, such as erecting fences and laying mines, in potential violation of the armistice that halted the 1950-53 Korean War.

The mine blast occurred while on a mission to clear a path for a joint investigation with the UNC into the North's border-hardening activities.

Kim voiced concern over possible clashes in the future if both sides continue to let their soldiers serve in the border area based on conflicting interpretations of the boundary lines, calling for "extraordinary measures" to resolve the issue.

"The damage will not be limited to any single side," he said.

Kim said that the recent increase in the North's border activities, and the warning broadcasts and warning shots from the South's side to make North Korean troops crossing the MDL retreat are directly linked to the current circumstances.

Under the Armistice Agreement signed in 1953, the UNC and North Korea installed 1,292 marker posts along the MDL to mark the ceasefire line.

However, most of them have deteriorated or been lost over time, leaving only about 200 identifiable markers as of now.

The South Korean military defines the MDL based on the mapping designated by the U.S. National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency. The UNC uses a different set of coordinates established through its own 2016 MDL project.

North Korea is believed to use its own version of the MDL based on its physical markers.

Since North Korean leader Kim Jong-un declared relations with the South as "two hostile states to each other," the North's military has stepped up border reinforcement work in a move seen as solidifying the regime's policy toward Seoul.

The South's military estimates the North has planted 960,000 land mines along the MDL since 2024, according to multiple lawmakers in Seoul.

South Korea has sought to open up dialogue with Pyongyang to discuss the discrepancies in the border demarcation and made a similar proposal for senior-level military talks last year. But Pyongyang has not responded to the proposal.

The UNC, which has legal jurisdiction on MDL management under the armistice, has shared the need to clarify the MDL baseline and reportedly conveyed its position to Pyongyang in the past.

Seoul informed the UNC of its plan to offer the military talks ahead of Friday's announcement, a defense ministry official told reporters.

"We did that prior (to the announcement), in accordance with protocol," he said, without elaborating further.

In a statement issued shortly after the announcement, the UNC reaffirmed its commitment to upholding the Armistice Agreement, and "reducing the risk of miscalculation and unintended escalation" along the MDL.

The UNC, however, declined to confirm whether it has reached the North Korean side about the South's dialogue offer, saying it does not publicly disclose its communication with Pyongyang.

The UNC maintains a hotline, known as the "pink phone," with the North's Korean People's Army, currently the only remaining communication channel between the two Koreas after Pyongyang severed all ties with Seoul. (Yonhap)

https://www.bnnbloomberg.ca/business/pol.heading: Canada works with EU on foreign aid, U.S. pulls back: Sarai
https://www.bnnbloomberg.ca/business/pol.body:
OTTAWA — Canada’s deepening ties with Europe could help fill some of the massive gaps left behind as the United States pulls back from foreign aid and embraces a “transactional” approach, says the secretary of state for international development.

“When we put all our heads together, I think the opportunities are endless,” Randeep Sarai told The Canadian Press.

He said this effort includes recent talks with the European Union on leveraging private dollars and philanthropy for aid, while maintaining some government funding for the world’s most vulnerable.

Sarai is overseeing a shift in foreign aid as the government of Prime Minister Mark Carney cuts back on global health spending and encourages more private funding in development projects.

Ottawa is cutting spending across government, seeking new trade partners and boosting the defence budget to make Canada less vulnerable to U.S. President Donald Trump’s tariffs and threats of annexation.

The Trump administration shut down the United States Agency for International Development, USAID, leading to what Harvard University researchers estimate to be hundreds of thousands of preventable deaths.

In April, the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development reported that the U.S. in 2025 accounted for 17 per cent of spending by rich countries on foreign aid, down from 30 per cent a year prior.

U.S. spending on foreign aid dropped by 57 per cent in 2025.

Most major donor states, including Canada, have cut back on aid funding. Ottawa spends about 1.6 per cent of its budget on foreign aid.

“Taxpayer dollars are very valuable. So if we can bring in the private sector along with them, the goal is (that) eventually the private sector will invest on their own. But initially, we’ll use the taxpayer dollars to entice them,” Sarai said.

Sarai added that Europe has looked to Carney for guidance on so-called blended finance because of his experience as a United Nations official.

Carney’s UN role was to advise governments on climate finance, including ways for governments to work with the private sector and philanthropists to transition to net-zero carbon emissions.

Ireland hosted a meeting of EU development ministers earlier this month and invited Canada to attend.

Sarai said much of the discussion in Dublin was about how to leverage private capital without abandoning support for the world’s most vulnerable people.

Sarai said Canada and European countries are also working with other nations with a reputation for robust foreign aid, including Japan, Korea and Gulf nations.

He said American officials have “come back, to some degree” on aid spending by funding vaccines for children in poor countries.

“Their aid has to benefit the American economy and American people,” Sarai said.

“They have very clear guidelines on that and transactional nature of it, but that’s their direction. So I would say it’s very different from the other G7 partners, but at least we know where we’re at.”

The push for more private dollars in aid has many critics.

Co-operation Canada, a coalition of most Canadian aid groups operating abroad, said the sector supports innovative funding, with some caveats.

“If we are to use public funds to incentivize private capital, then there need to be some guardrails around … that we’re we’re using our public funds in the most efficient way possible,” said Paul Farran, the group’s advocacy director.

He said aid dollars shouldn’t be used to subsidize endeavours that the private sector wouldn’t have otherwise funded.

“Our international assistance should first and foremost be used to alleviate poverty and inequalities,” Farran said.

Sarai said Canada is not going to surrender its support for the world’s poorest to market forces.

He said that applies to Canada’s programming in the 32 nations the UN describes as the world’s least developed countries, as well as projects that focus on sexual health and reproductive rights.

He said the government has a different approach in high-growth countries, where it pursues “mutual economic prosperity” through projects that benefit Canadian companies and investors while creating jobs abroad.

“The Vietnams, Indonesias, Philippines in the world, we believe that they can now take care of those areas themselves. We don’t need to invest in those particular areas for them,” he said.

Sarai cited a new aid project in Thailand which will see Canada’s development finance institution FinDev lend cash for microloans to women in rural areas looking to launch or expand businesses.

Canada is lending roughly $85 million, which is being matched by $280 million from the Japanese bank SMBC and the Asian Development Bank.

Last month, The House finance committee, which has a majority of Liberal MPs, called on Carney last month to provide predictable and clear aid funding in the Nov. 5 budget.

Aid groups told the committee that the federal government says its supports for refugees inside Canada amount to more than 17 per cent of its total development assistance. While that’s a standard reporting practice for western countries, the aid groups said it makes it hard to tell how much Canadian cash is actually going abroad.

The MPs on the committee argued aid spending should be “guided by poverty and fragility” and should have “increasing transparency in the international assistance envelope.”

The MPs also urged Canada to “reaffirm gender equality and women’s economic empowerment as drivers of poverty reduction and, therefore, as central priorities.” Carney caused confusion a year ago by suggesting Canada no longer has a feminist foreign policy.

Co-operation Canada supports those calls and is urging Carney to reverse cuts to global health programs.

Farran said Canada should earmark $5.5 billion annually for “core” development aid abroad, which would boost funding for things like building schools or helping women advocate for political rights.

He also said Ottawa owes the public more clarity on how it is spending foreign aid and where it’s cutting back.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 23, 2026.

Dylan Robertson, The Canadian Press

https://www.bnnbloomberg.ca/business/pol.heading: Mark Carney in Turkiye mentions Canadian bid on nuclear plant
https://www.bnnbloomberg.ca/business/pol.body:
ISTANBUL -- Prime Minister Mark Carney said Friday a Canadian company has a real shot at winning a lucrative tender to supply nuclear energy to Turkiye -- a prospect he said was remote a year ago.

Carney was meeting with Turkish business leaders in Istanbul Friday, a day after he announced a new strategic partnership between Canada and Turkiye to deepen co-operation on a range of files.

Energy is one of the pillars of that agreement and Carney said the AtkinsRealis bid to supply two planned Turkish power plants with the Candu nuclear reactor now has “good chances” of succeeding. He added it would have been a long-shot a year ago.

“We’re in negotiations, and those negotiations are getting more intense. Probably from here to the end of the year, or around COP 31, it will be a decision for the Turkish government,” Carney told reporters in French.

COP31 is the United Nations Climate Change Conference, set for Antalya, Turkiye from Nov. 9 to 20.

“Candu has a chance,” Carney added. “Yes, there’s competition. But we have the quality of the technology, of the financing, and a true partnership with business in this country with Canada.”

Ian Edwards, president and CEO of AtkinsRealis, confirmed in a LinkedIn post on Friday that he is also in Turkey this week.

He thanked Carney and Natural Resources Minister Tim Hodgson, who is also on the trip, for “their partnership and continued support in advancing this important opportunity for Canadian nuclear energy.”

Edwards said AtkinsRealis is conducting a feasibility study for the potential build-out of Candu reactors at Sinop, a city in Turkey on the Black Sea proposed for the site of a new power plant.

In June, Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand welcomed her Turkish counterpart to Canada. During the trip, Turkish officials toured the Darlington nuclear facility in Ontario.

Canada’s nuclear strategy was released a week before the June trip.

The plan looks to sell more Candu reactors around the world and sets a goal of entering at least four new international markets by 2040. It also seeks to “engage six to 10 new nuclear entrant markets over a 15-year horizon, cementing Canada as their partner of choice.”

The push to sell Candu to new markets is an attempt to establish Canada as a reliable uranium export partner and to use nuclear energy as a geopolitical lever.

The prime minister said while contract decisions are ultimately made business-to-business, his role in Istanbul is to share how the Canadian market has become more welcoming to foreign firms and investors.

“We’ve made some fairly big changes in terms of the tax regime in Canada, the speed with which investment decisions are (being made), the way we’re partnering with a broader group of countries ... those are a lot of changes at the same time,” Carney said.

“You have to go out and explain to people what’s changed.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 23, 2026.

With files from Nick Murray in Ottawa

ISTANBUL/OTTAWA -- Prime Minister Mark Carney said he is “disappointed” in ongoing allegations from U.S. Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra, who is accusing Canadian politicians of interfering in the upcoming U.S. midterm elections.

“There is no merit to these claims, so I’ll call it out that way,” Carney said while speaking to reporters in Istanbul on Friday. “I’m disappointed that their envoy sees that it’s his role to make these suggestions.”

Carney added that Canada is “very careful” to make sure the country “not be seen to” interfere and referenced Canada’s “deep diplomatic presence” in the United States.

Earlier this month, Hoekstra warned Canadian leaders to stay out of American politics while speaking to “The Really Big Show” podcast and accused several Canadian politicians, including Industry Minister Mélanie Joly, of meddling in close U.S. midterm races.

The U.S. Embassy to Canada, meanwhile, released a fact sheet this week outlining alleged instances of foreign interference in 2025 and 2026, pointing to Joly along with Ontario Premier Doug Ford and Liberal MP Anthony Housefather.

All this comes as Global Affairs Canada reportedly issued an advisory to Canadian diplomats based in the U.S. to avoid appearing with midterm candidates.

Carney said that guidance came well before Hoekstra’s allegations.

“Our global affairs group, well in advance of these fact sheets and allegations, has been reminding everybody: be careful who you are even seen with, who you’re physically in the same place as, so that such unsubstantiated allegations can’t be made,” he said.

U.S. President Donald Trump is expected to face a big test during the U.S. midterm elections on Nov. 3. as several American polls show his approval falling to record lows.

The midterms happen midway through a four-year presidential election cycle and could change the balance of political power in Washington.

Asked if he thinks the U.S. will blame Canada for poor midterm results for the Republican Party and respond with additional tariffs, Carney said, “I don’t see that coming to pass,” but added he “can’t predict what the United States is going to do.”

The US is reducing embassy staff across the Middle East after intelligence officials warned that Iranian plots against Americans have reached advanced stages.

ERBIL (Kurdistan24) - The United States is reducing diplomatic personnel across the Middle East after intelligence agencies warned that Iran has intensified planning for attacks against Americans and that some plots have reached advanced stages, according to U.S. officials cited by The New York Times.

The report, by Edward Wong, Jonathan Swan and Julian E. Barnes, said diplomats and other federal employees across the region have been placed on heightened alert, with Washington ordering personnel to leave Saudi Arabia and adjusting staffing at other diplomatic missions.

The intelligence assessment was conveyed Friday to Secretary of State Marco Rubio in a memorandum from Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, according to the Times.

The memo warned that Iranian efforts to target U.S. personnel had increased substantially and that lethal plots against American citizens had reached "advanced stages" in the Middle East and some other countries.

U.S. officials told the newspaper that agencies now assess the threat to Americans in the region and elsewhere as the highest since the U.S.-Iran war began in February.

The Trump administration confirmed the existence of the intelligence memo through a U.S. official, according to the report.

President Donald Trump and senior administration officials have been receiving regular briefings on the threat, which U.S. intelligence believes extends beyond the Middle East.

Officials cited by the Times said analysts have spent roughly three weeks examining intelligence concerning possible attacks against American officials, including ambassadors.

Some intelligence indicated that Iran may have operatives inside the United States, while potential targets in Europe were also being examined, according to the report.

One U.S. official, however, cautioned that Tehran's ambitions may exceed its actual ability to carry out attacks in the United States or other countries outside the region.

The allegations are assessments by U.S. intelligence officials. The material does not include an Iranian response to the latest claims.

The State Department said it continually reassesses embassy staffing according to changing security conditions.

A U.S. official told the Times that both Iranian attack plots and threats from Yemen's Houthi forces were influencing staffing decisions at diplomatic missions.

Many U.S. embassies in the Middle East are already operating under what the State Department calls "restricted operating status," allowing Washington greater flexibility to move personnel without repeatedly issuing public departure notices.

On Wednesday, the department ordered nonessential employees and family members to leave Saudi Arabia.

Officials said other missions in the region have also been quietly reducing or rotating personnel, with the latest moves directly connected to the new intelligence.

The security measures come as Washington and Israel continue weighing their next steps against Iran.

The Times reported earlier this week that U.S. and Israeli officials have developed plans for another round of strikes after the Nov. 3 U.S. midterm elections, though Trump has not made a final decision.

Trump said Friday that he had no information about a possible attack on Iran this weekend after U.S. envoy Tom Barrack said such a strike could "absolutely" occur.

Trump nevertheless kept the possibility of future military action open, telling supporters in Florida: "We may do another little Epic Fury."

The president has also previously indicated that large-scale military action would not take place before the midterms.

The current intelligence alert follows earlier Iranian threats that prompted U.S. military precautions.

According to the Times, all 12 U.S. B-1 bombers stationed at RAF Fairford in southern England were withdrawn in early October after commanders received information concerning a potential Iranian threat to the base.

Diplomatic staffing has also been repeatedly adjusted since the war began.

After the United States and Israel struck Iran on Feb. 28, Tehran responded with missile and drone attacks across the region.

On March 2, Washington ordered nonessential personnel to leave diplomatic missions in Iraq, Jordan and Bahrain. Similar measures were later taken in Saudi Arabia following attacks affecting Riyadh and nearby areas.

Türkiye, meanwhile, has warned against another military escalation.

Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said Friday that any renewed attack on Iran would intensify regional tensions and argued that military action would not provide a solution.

He also called for the Strait of Hormuz to reopen as soon as possible, citing the damage the conflict and shipping disruption have inflicted on international energy markets.

The latest U.S. security measures therefore come at a particularly sensitive point: Washington is considering its military options, regional governments are warning against escalation, and U.S. intelligence agencies are simultaneously raising their assessment of the threat to American personnel.

WASHINGTON, Oct. 23 (Yonhap) -- The U.S. Army has activated an air defense battalion in Guam to bolster the island's defenses against regional missile threats, including those posed by North Korea and China, a U.S. military news outlet reported Friday.

The 3rd Battalion, 43rd Air Defense Artillery Regiment, held an activation ceremony on Oct. 16 at Andersen Air Force Base in Guam and will assume the air defense responsibilities previously carried out by Task Force Talon, according to USNI News.

Task Force Talon began its rotational mission in 2013 to counter potential North Korean ballistic missile threats, but its responsibilities have since expanded amid China's growing missile capabilities, the report said.

The newly activated battalion is expected to operate Patriot, Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) and Intermediate Fires Protection Capability (IFPC) systems as part of a layered defense network against ballistic and cruise missiles, aircraft and drones.

"Guam's strategic location makes it an important part of U.S. military operations throughout the region by supporting joint force operations while making air and missile defense a critical part of protecting the forces and infrastructure needed to support those missions," the Army told USNI News.

According to the Army, the transition from a rotational task force to a battalion reflects the Pentagon's commitment to establishing permanent air defense capabilities in the Indo-Pacific.

Guam, a strategically important U.S. territory in the western Pacific, currently relies on THAAD launchers and U.S. Navy Aegis-equipped warships on an as-needed basis for air and missile defense, according to the report.

Washington (United States) (AFP) – US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Friday called for Cubans to make "discreet" contact with the American intelligence services as Washington seeks to force an end to the island's communist government.

Issued on: 24/10/2026 - 01:25Modified: 24/10/2026 - 05:09

For months, President Donald Trump and other senior US officials have openly hinted at a military intervention or takeover of Cuba, ramping up economic, political and legal pressure on the country.

"To those who seek to create positive change in Cuba -- now is the time," Rubio said on social media.

"The disappointment of failed promises, corruption, and the privileged lives of only a few; seize this opportunity to create the change you desire through a discrete partnership with the CIA."

The unusual post appeared to confirm that the CIA is currently active in Cuba after a long history of covert operations including backing the disastrous Bay of Pigs invasion in 1961.

The call was mocked by Cuban officials.

"Now the United States is resorting to public recruitment for the CIA," Cuban Deputy Foreign Minister Carlos Fernandez de Cossio wrote on X.

"There must be a great deal of desperation or misery within the agency for it to be forced to sell its services like a tube of toothpaste."

The CIA later uploaded a video to X offering instructions in Spanish for those who believe they have information of interest to the intelligence agency, encouraging them to first and foremost visit an official US installation in person if they can safely travel to one.

For those hoping to contact the CIA online via the cia.gov website, the agency instructed users to access the internet on a secure network like a VPN using a private browser and a burner email account unassociated with any personal details.

Those sharing information should be prepared to include their city, job, level of access and contact information with their message.

Trump, speaking at a rally in Florida earlier Friday, underlined his ambitions to impose regime change in Cuba.

"Those beautiful (US military) ships will pass Cuba. We'll have one of them stop about 50 yards off the coast," he said. "They'll raise up their hands. And then we're going to send Marco Rubio in to finish up the deal."

Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodriguez quickly dismissed Trump's threats.

"Our coastline is full of beautiful beaches, but there are also razor-sharp limestone spikes, an inhospitable environment for those who make it to our shores with hostile purposes and lust for domination," he posted.

In the latest US move against the Cuban leadership, Florida's top prosecutor this week announced an arrest warrant for former president Raul Castro on state murder charges that echo a federal indictment unveiled earlier this year.

Castro, 95, is wanted on murder charges connected to the 1996 shooting down of two civilian aircraft from "Brothers to the Rescue," an organization assisting Cubans fleeing to the US state by sea.

Castro, brother of the late revolutionary leader and US nemesis Fidel Castro, was indicted on federal charges related to the incident in May.

Trump previously seized on a US indictment to justify military action that toppled Venezuela's then-president Nicolas Maduro, a staunch ally of the Cuban authorities.

Current Cuban President Miguel Diaz-Canel has said the US federal indictment against Castro has "no legal basis" and was an attempt "to justify the folly of a military aggression against Cuba."

Washington also imposed a de facto energy blockade on Cuba in January, threatening to sanction any country that supplies fuel to the island of 9.4 million people.

https://breakingdefense.com/2026/10/spac.heading: Space Force reveals first 6 'operational' contracts for civil reserve support in space monitoring - Breaking Defense
https://breakingdefense.com/2026/10/spac.body:
WASHINGTON — The Space Force has awarded what the service calls the first “operational” contracts under its still-nascent Commercial Augmentation Space Reserve (CASR) initiative to six space monitoring firms, Space Systems Command (SSC) announced.

The contracts are short term and designed to test military demand while the command’s Commercial Space Office (COMSO) continues to wrestle with thorny legal issues that have bedeviled the program from its launch in 2023.

The six new contracts — issued to Australian firm EOS Space Systems, Canada’s NorthStar Earth and Space, InTrack Radar, Anduril (via its acquisition of ExoAnalytic), Slingshot Aerospace, and LeoLabs — are worth a total of $1.37 million, an SSC spokesperson told Breaking Defense.

CASR is the Space Force’s planned version of the Civil Reserve Air Fleet (CRAF) for leveraging commercial airlines to support military logistics operations when needed, managed by US Transportation Command (TRANSCOM). The concept is that commercial space firms could be called upon in wartime to surge delivery of satellite-derived capabilities.

According to SSC’s Thursday press release, the contracts were let through the “General Services Administration contract framework” used by the Joint Commercial Operations cell to buy commercial data and services. Industry sources who have received similar contracts from the JCO cell have said they tend to run for no more than six months.

The new contracts follow COMSO’s March 2025 award of $1.1 million in three-month pilot contracts to four unnamed companies, first reported by Breaking Defense. Those awards were designed to test out the contracting processes and the CASR framework agreement for interested firms, rather than provide operational data.

According to reports by Air & Space Forces Magazine and Space News, COMSO head Col. Tim Tremillo told reporters during the annual Space Industry Days conference held Oct. 19-22 in Los Angeles that the initial operational awards were meant to provide a short-term boost in space domain awareness data, with the idea that these initial contracts would allow the service to judge military demand. He also made it clear that he expects the CASR program to expand both to more companies and more mission areas.

The goal of such weaponization is to tie warfighter needs to the RDT&E cycle.

However, given the small dollar values and short contract duration of the new contracts, it is hard to see how companies will be enticed to join up, said Clayton Swope, deputy director of the Aerospace Security Project at the Center for Strategic and International Studies.

“It will be hard for companies to build capacity and capability at scale for use during a crisis if they aren’t paid to do so today. Companies otherwise will not make investments for infrastructure that sits unused and idle, ready for on-demand use, if they are not compensated to build and also maintain that surge capability. Companies do not build extra capacity for sport—it costs money,” he told Breaking Defense today.

Meanwhile, COMSO has yet to develop contractual arrangements that deal with key legal and financial issues that are critical to enticing commercial space companies to join CASR.

The first issue revolves around when and if the US government will have the right to turn off a CASR partner’s services to other customers during a conflict ― a power often referred to as “shutter control.” Companies worry that they could be accused of breach of contract by existing customers if that right were exercised by Washington, and that potential customers (particularly foreign governments) will be scared off.

The second outstanding issue is the question of whether the Pentagon will be willing to indemnify partner firms against financial losses whose satellites are damaged or destroyed during a conflict.
